HoMe: Toward Practical Harness Optimization
of Memory Systems for AI Assistants

Yifei Xu Email: mailto:xuyf@sjtu.edu.cnxuyf    Li Yu Email: mailto:shenyy@sjtu.edu.cnshenyy    Zhaoyang Liu Email: mailto:linyun@sjtu.edu.cnlinyun    Ce Wang Email: mailto:lphuang@sjtu.edu.cnlphuang@sjtu.edu.cn    Sen Huang Email: mailto:jingmu.lzy@alibaba-inc.comjingmu.lzy@alibaba-inc.commailto:meih@pku.edu.cnmeih@pku.edu.cn    Yanyan Shen ††thanks: Corresponding author.    Yun Lin    Linpeng Huang    Hong Mei Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University Alibaba Group Peking University
Abstract

The behavior of memory systems for long-running AI assistants is governed by a harness, which consists of the code, prompts, and configurations for memory construction, maintenance, retrieval, and answer generation. However, optimizing the harness of a memory system remains largely manual, and unrestricted editing alone does not ensure structural improvements. In this paper, we introduce HoMe, an evaluation-driven framework that iteratively evaluates candidate harnesses and derives each new candidate from any previously evaluated harness by editing any part of it. HoMe combines session-level memory versioning with execution traces to identify shared failure mechanisms across cases and localize them to the responsible sessions and harness components. It encourages early structural exploration through candidate gating and reduces evaluation cost through smoke tests, adaptive sampling, and the reuse of constructed memory. We validate HoMe with the open-source memory system ReMe on two large-scale long-horizon memory benchmarks, LongMemEval-S and BEAM. With six formal candidate evaluations per benchmark, after a full initial evaluation, HoMe discovers harnesses that improve end-task performance over the originally strong harness while consuming far fewer query-time tokens. The code is available at https://github.com/agentscope-ai/ReMe.

1 Introduction

Long-running AI assistants accumulate conversational and episodic experience through continued interaction, and they depend on a memory system to turn that experience into consistent and personalized behavior across sessions (Packer et al., 2023; Chhikara et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025; Zhong et al., 2023; Wang and Chen, 2025). In practice, memory is not merely persistent storage but a standalone system built around a language model, exposing interfaces for a target agent to store and retrieve information as needed. Many such systems are file-native, i.e., maintaining memory as files (Zhou et al., 2026). Three components govern the system behavior: the code that implements memory construction, maintenance, retrieval, and answer generation, along with associated evaluation and recovery mechanisms; the prompts that instruct the language model at each stage; and the configurations that determine the memory schemas, indexes, thresholds, etc. We call this collection of code, prompts, and configurations the harness of a memory system.

Different AI assistants often have different demands on memory data management. For example, a medical assistant stores symptom histories and medication details that must be preserved faithfully, whereas a scheduling assistant stores event states that are revised repeatedly and should be superseded rather than accumulated (Wu et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2026). Hence, the harness of a memory system must be optimized before deployment to achieve acceptable results on application-specific evaluations (Yao et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026). The same effort is required again after deployment, because growing interaction histories and shifting user behavior expose failures that could not be anticipated beforehand. This process is extremely time-consuming due to the huge search space and is still carried out manually, which raises a timely and important question: how can the harness of a memory system be optimized automatically?

Prior work has largely treated the harness of a memory system as an artifact to be designed. Most efforts propose new architectures and retrieval strategies (Packer et al., 2023; Gutiérrez et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025; Rasmussen et al., 2025; Pan et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026), or grant the target agent control over memory operations, such as deciding what to write and when to retrieve (Zhang et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2025). Recent work automates memory harness optimization. EvolveMem (Liu et al., 2026b) optimizes retrieval strategies through autonomous research. MemPro (Liu et al., 2026c) optimizes memory construction and retrieval, largely delegating failure diagnosis and revision planning to its evolving agent. MStar (Pan et al., 2026) jointly optimizes memory schemas, read and write code, and instructions through population-based search. However, full-harness editing alone does not ensure structural exploration. In our ReMe-based optimization experiments, all candidates proposed by MemPro modify prompts or parameters, despite executable-code edits being permitted. This motivates explicit mechanisms that connect failures across cases to the responsible harness components and guide structural exploration under a limited budget.

In this paper, we move one step further and introduce HoMe, an evaluation-driven framework that guides free-form memory-harness optimization through cross-case mechanism diagnosis and early structural exploration. Our framework is inspired by Meta-Harness (Lee et al., 2026), a general scheme that delegates harness optimization to a code agent, which reads a harness with its evaluation evidence and returns a revised harness. At each iteration, HoMe diagnoses the optimization history, including all the harnesses proposed so far, the memories they constructed, and their evaluation results. It then performs arbitrary edits to propose a new candidate harness and evaluates it accordingly. The loop continues until it reaches the iteration limit and selects a final harness.

However, applying such a flexible harness optimization scheme to a memory system for AI assistants is not viable, because the system operates over a long horizon (e.g., exceeding thousands of messages (Tavakoli et al., 2025)), which raises two challenges. First, accurate diagnosis is essential yet difficult (Yan et al., 2026). A query is answered from memory accumulated over hundreds of preceding sessions, and a low score may originate in how a session was segmented and written, in a later revision that overwrote relevant content, or in the retrieval procedure that selected what was returned. Without locating the responsible part of the harness, there is little guidance on what to change, and iterations are easily wasted on unrelated edits. Second, evaluation is prohibitively expensive. For each candidate harness, evaluation constructs memory over all preceding sessions, answers the evaluation queries, and invokes a judge on every case, where a case comprises one or several queries. Evaluation therefore dominates the runtime of the optimization process.

For failed queries, HoMe reads the execution trace to determine at which stage the evidence was lost, whether it was never written, later overwritten, or stored but not retrieved. It inspects the implicated sessions’ diffs to confirm the cause and traces the failure to the responsible harness component. We further aggregate the diagnoses across cases to distinguish recurring harness defects from isolated failures. Second, HoMe lowers the evaluation cost along three axes: smoke tests reject broken harnesses, while candidate gating reserves early evaluations for structural exploration; adaptive sampling restricts each evaluation to the most informative cases, reducing the number of cases per evaluation; and constructed memory is reused when a candidate leaves memory construction behavior unchanged, reducing the construction cost per case. We also extend version control to the optimization itself: the harness edits and the diagnosis reports of every iteration are committed together, so that each iteration builds on prior attempts rather than rediscovering them.

We implement HoMe on the open-source memory system ReMe (Cao et al., 2026) and evaluate it on the long-horizon benchmarks LongMemEval-S (Wu et al., 2024) and BEAM (Tavakoli et al., 2025). Evaluating only six candidate harnesses per benchmark in several hours, HoMe discovers harnesses that outperform the original one by 2.8 and 5.4 percentage points (pp) in evaluation score while reducing query-time token consumption by 59% and 41%, respectively. Compared with MemPro, HoMe improves scores by 10.4 pp on LongMemEval-S and 1.1 pp on BEAM, while reducing query-time tokens by 81.5% and 7.6%, respectively. The harness optimized on BEAM-100K also remains effective on BEAM-1M conversations, which are about 8×8\times longer on average than those in BEAM-100K, showing it generalizes across memory scales. To summarize, our major contributions are the following.

∙\bullet We introduce HoMe , an evaluation-driven framework that guides memory-harness optimization through cross-case mechanism diagnosis and early structural exploration, enabling effective revisions under a limited evaluation budget.

∙\bullet We identify two challenges that arise in the long-horizon setting, namely accurate diagnosis and evaluation cost, and address them through session-level memory versioning with diff-based diagnosis for the former, and candidate gating, adaptive sampling, and memory reuse for the latter.

∙\bullet We evaluate HoMe on ReMe using LongMemEval-S and BEAM. By evaluating only six candidate harnesses per benchmark, HoMe identifies harnesses that score higher than the strong original harness while consuming fewer query-time tokens. The harness optimized on BEAM-100K also generalizes to BEAM-1M, where conversations are about 8×8\times longer on average.

2 Preliminaries

We consider a file-backed memory system built around a language model that serves a target agent through two interfaces: memory construction and retrieval. Let 𝒮=(s1,…,sT)\mathcal{S}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{T}) denote a chronologically ordered history of sessions, where each session is a sequence of interaction messages. Let mtm_{t} denote the persistent memory state after session sts_{t}, including the memory files and indexes. Starting from an initial state m0m_{0}, the system processes the history and answers a query qq as follows:

mt=Ch​(mt−1,st),t∈[1,T],rq=Rh​(mT,q),aq=Ah​(q,rq).m_{t}=C_{h}(m_{t-1},s_{t}),t\in[1,T],\quad r_{q}=R_{h}(m_{T},q),\quad a_{q}=A_{h}(q,r_{q}). (1)

Here CC denotes the construction process; RR denotes the retrieval process; and rqr_{q} denotes the information retrieved by the target agent AA, which produces the answer aqa_{q}.

Harness of a memory system. The harness of a memory system is a triple h=(c,p,θ)∈ℋh=(c,p,\theta)\in\mathcal{H}, where cc denotes the executable code, pp denotes the prompts, and θ\theta denotes the configuration values such as memory schemas, indexing options, and thresholds. These components jointly determine memory construction, retrieval, and answer generation, i.e., ChC_{h}, RhR_{h}, and AhA_{h}, including their language model calls, internal control flow, and recovery mechanisms. The search space ℋ\mathcal{H} consists of the harnesses that preserve the interfaces in Eq. 1, whereas the language model remains fixed and lies outside hh.

Harness evaluation. Let 𝒟={xi}i=1N\mathcal{D}=\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} denote the set of application-specific evaluation cases. Each case xi=(𝒮i,𝒬i,𝒢i)x_{i}=(\mathcal{S}_{i},\mathcal{Q}_{i},\mathcal{G}_{i}) comprises a session history 𝒮i=(si,1,…,si,Ti)\mathcal{S}_{i}=(s_{i,1},\ldots,s_{i,T_{i}}), a nonempty set of queries 𝒬i\mathcal{Q}_{i} grounded in that history, and a set of ground-truth answers. Applying hh to case xix_{i} according to Eq. 1 yields an answer ai,qha^{h}_{i,q} for every q∈𝒬iq\in\mathcal{Q}_{i}, which a fixed external judge JJ scores as yi,q​(h)=J⁡(q,ai,qh,gi,q)∈[0,1]y_{i,q}(h)=J(q,a^{h}_{i,q},g_{i,q})\in[0,1]. Evaluating a candidate harness hbh_{b} on 𝒟\mathcal{D} produces:

(𝐲b,𝐞b,κb)=Eval⁡(hb;𝒟),(\mathbf{y}_{b},\mathbf{e}_{b},\kappa_{b})=\operatorname{Eval}(h_{b};\mathcal{D}), (2)

where 𝐲b\mathbf{y}_{b} collects the query-level scores; 𝐞b\mathbf{e}_{b} is the evaluation trajectory comprising the query execution logs and the intermediate memory states; and κb\kappa_{b} records query-stage token consumption, i.e., the average number of tokens consumed per query for retrieval and answer generation.

Harness optimization. In this paper, we study the iterative optimization of the harness of a memory system. Starting from an initial harness h0h_{0}, each iteration bb uses the accumulated evaluation history 𝒪b=((,,,,,,,))j=0b\mathcal{O}_{b}=\bigl((h_{j},\mathbf{y}_{j},\mathbf{e}_{j},\kappa_{j})\bigr)_{j=0}^{b} and the evaluation data 𝒟\mathcal{D} to propose the next candidate:

hb+1=Π⁡(𝒪b,𝒟),h_{b+1}=\Pi(\mathcal{O}_{b},\mathcal{D}), (3)

where Π\Pi denotes the candidate-generation procedure. Under a budget of BB iterations, the objective is to identify h∗∈{h0,…,hB}h^{*}\in\{h_{0},\ldots,h_{B}\} with the highest score on the complete evaluation set DD, while favoring lower query-stage token consumption κ\kappa over expanded context or tool-use budgets. HoMe approximates this objective from accumulated evidence without fully evaluating every candidate.

3 Diagnosable and Efficient Harness Optimization

3.1 The HoMe Framework

HoMe is an evaluation-driven framework that optimizes the harness of a file-native memory system. As shown in Figure 1, it consists of three major components. The Developer Agents take the role that human developers play in manual harness optimization: they diagnose the failures of evaluated candidates and edit a harness to produce a new candidate. The Experiment Manager records all candidates and their evaluation results, controls the Developer Agents’ access to tools, and decides how each candidate is evaluated. The Evaluation Environment executes evaluations in isolated sandboxes. In each iteration, the Developer Agents submit a candidate, the Experiment Manager screens it and plans its evaluation, the Evaluation Environment evaluates it, and the Experiment Manager records the results for subsequent iterations. In HoMe, the Developer Agents and the Experiment Manager jointly realize Π\Pi in Eq. 3, and the Evaluation Environment computes Eval\operatorname{Eval} in Eq. 2 for each candidate admitted to formal evaluation.

Developer agents. The Developer Agents consist of an Optimizer Agent that generates candidates and a Diagnoser Agent that attributes failures to memory construction, retrieval, or answering (Section 3.2). All candidates originate from the initial harness h0h_{0}, which is evaluated on the full 𝒟\mathcal{D} and stored as the root commit of a Git repository maintained by the Experiment Manager. We call this repository the harness repository, and each of its branches tests one optimization hypothesis. In each iteration, the Diagnoser Agent reads the optimization history 𝒪b\mathcal{O}_{b} together with the diagnoses attached to earlier commits and then diagnoses the failures of the most recently evaluated candidate hbh_{b}. Based on these diagnoses, the Optimizer Agent selects an evaluated candidate hjh_{j} with j≤bj\leq b as the parent of the next candidate. The choice of parent determines how the search proceeds: extending the latest candidate on a branch refines the hypothesis of that branch; starting a new branch pursues a different hypothesis and may begin from an earlier candidate when the current hypothesis fails to improve performance; and merging two branches combines changes that address complementary failures. HoMe leaves this choice to the Optimizer Agent.

Experiment manager. The Experiment Manager maintains the harness repository, controls the evaluation of each candidate, and provides the Developer Agents with a unified tool interface for code inspection within a permission boundary. A candidate is admitted to evaluation only if it passes a smoke test (Section 3.3). A rejected candidate is returned to the Optimizer Agent with the rejection reason and consumes no formal evaluation budget. To reduce the evaluation cost for an admitted candidate hb+1h_{b+1}, the Experiment Manager judiciously samples an evaluation subset 𝒟b+1⊆𝒟\mathcal{D}_{b+1}\subseteq\mathcal{D} or reuses the cases and memory states from the nearest evaluated ancestor with an equivalent construction process. It then evaluates hb+1h_{b+1} on 𝒟b+1\mathcal{D}_{b+1} and returns the evaluation record (𝐲b+1,𝐞b+1,κb+1)(\mathbf{y}_{b+1},\mathbf{e}_{b+1},\kappa_{b+1}). We refer to this step as a formal evaluation, which consumes one unit of the budget BB. Since the repository provides complete provenance for every candidate and records their evaluation trajectories and diagnostic information, each iteration can build upon previous attempts while retaining the evidence and reasoning that motivated earlier harness revisions.

Evaluation environment. The Evaluation Environment executes smoke tests and formal evaluations. In a formal evaluation of hb+1h_{b+1}, each case xi∈𝒟b+1x_{i}\in\mathcal{D}_{b+1} runs in an isolated Docker sandbox that performs memory construction, retrieval, answering, and scoring with the fixed judge JJ. All cases run concurrently, and a pool of warm sandboxes reduces startup overhead. During construction, the sandbox commits the memory files after every session and thus produces the memory repository of xix_{i}. When the Experiment Manager permits memory reuse for xix_{i}, the sandbox restores the memory constructed for the selected ancestor and runs only retrieval, answering, and scoring using the same persisted memory state as that ancestor.

3.2 Long-Horizon Failure Diagnosis

In each iteration, the Developer Agents analyzes the failed cases of the most recently evaluated candidate hbh_{b}, where a case fails if any of its queries receives a low score. For the failed cases, it identifies the cause of the failure and the responsible part of the harness. However, a low evaluation score does not reveal the cause. The required information may never have been written to memory, may have been corrupted or deleted by later maintenance, may be present in memory but not retrieved, or may be retrieved but used incorrectly during answering. A direct diagnosis must therefore examine the evaluation trajectory of the case, which consists of the query execution logs and the intermediate memory states (see Eq. 1). The query execution logs are typically short, but the intermediate memory states span many processed sessions. These states are expensive to examine in full and can far exceed the context window of a single agent. The difficulty is compounded because an evaluation often contains many failed cases. HoMe addresses these difficulties with three designs.

Session-level memory versioning. This design makes the intermediate memory states compact and inspectable on demand. During construction, the Evaluation Environment commits the memory files of each case xix_{i} to a Git repository after every session. The commits of this memory repository are checkpoints of the intermediate memory states mi,tm_{i,t}, and the diff between two consecutive checkpoints records exactly what one session changed. An agent can therefore retrieve any intermediate state or any single-session change without reading the entire history or loading every checkpoint into its context.

Trajectory-guided attribution. An agent attributes failures by tracing a case’s evaluation trajectory backward from each low-scoring query qq and using session-level memory checkpoints to inspect relevant changes (Wang et al., 2026; Zhai et al., 2025). It first checks whether the retrieved information rqr_{q} and the final memory state mi,Tim_{i,T_{i}} contain the information required by qq. If rqr_{q} contains the information, the failure lies in answering. If only mi,Tim_{i,T_{i}} contains it, the failure lies in retrieval. Otherwise, the failure lies in construction. For a construction failure, the agent locates the source sessions si,ts_{i,t} that contain the required information and inspects the diffs between mi,t−1m_{i,t-1} and mi,tm_{i,t} to determine whether it was written to memory. If it was, the agent follows subsequent changes to the files that stored it to identify the session in which it was corrupted or deleted. The agent summarizes its findings in a compact case diagnosis that records each failure’s cause, any implicated sessions, and the responsible harness component, together with the evidence supporting the attribution.

Parallel case diagnosis. A dedicated Diagnoser Agent investigates failed cases and produces a diagnosis report for the Optimizer Agent. This division of labor keeps detailed case investigations out of the Optimizer Agent’s context so it can focus on mechanism-level revisions to the harness. The Diagnoser Agent uses a map-reduce workflow. In the map phase, it invokes a batch tool that runs Case Study Agents in parallel. Each agent applies trajectory-guided attribution to one case in an independent context and returns a compact case diagnosis. This reduces latency and avoids reprocessing earlier case histories. In the reduce phase, the Diagnoser Agent compares the diagnoses and looks for corroborating evidence across cases before inferring a shared cause. It groups the case diagnoses by failure mechanism and prioritizes the groups supported by the most cases to identify shared harness defects. This helps distinguish recurring harness failures from case-specific effects and limits the influence of individual diagnostic errors on the overall attribution. The diagnosis report links the supported shared causes to the responsible harness code.

3.3 Efficient Evaluation of Candidate Harness

The overall evaluation cost depends on three factors: the number of formal evaluations, the number of cases per evaluation, and the average cost per case. HoMe reduces these factors through smoke test and candidate gating, adaptive case and query sampling, and construction-aware memory reuse.

Smoke test and candidate gating. HoMe screens a candidate harness with two checks that cost far less than a formal evaluation. First, it runs a smoke test that executes the candidate on real cases deterministically truncated to a few sessions and queries. This rejects candidates with implementation failures such as runtime exceptions. Second, we develop a gate that decides whether a candidate may enter formal evaluation. We observe that an unconstrained optimizer initially proposes many candidates that edit only prompts or configurations, because such edits are cheap to produce. Such edits can bias search toward local fixes rather than shared failure mechanisms. Later code changes may also invalidate early prompt or configuration tuning. We therefore prioritize structural exploration before refinement, devoting the first B/2B/2 budget units to exploration and the rest to refinement. During exploration, the gate prioritizes changes to runtime mechanisms, such as memory representation, construction, and retrieval, while also admitting necessary fixes to execution failures. The gate inspects the candidate diff and affected runtime paths, rejecting prompt-only or parameter-only tuning and superficial code edits that leave information flow and control flow unchanged. During refinement, the gate is lifted, allowing candidates that modify only prompts or configurations as well as those that continue to modify code, building on the mechanisms and evaluation evidence established during exploration.

Adaptive case and query sampling. To reduce the cost of each formal evaluation, HoMe restricts it to a subset 𝒟b+1⊆𝒟\mathcal{D}_{b+1}\subseteq\mathcal{D} selected by an adaptive sampler. The sampler treats each case and query as a sampling unit, indexed by vv. Intuitively, recently failed or persistently low-scoring units reveal the limitations of the current harness more often than units that consistently pass. However, evaluation is stochastic, and harness changes can cause correct units to regress. The sampler therefore prioritizes high-loss units while preserving coverage of the remaining units. This evolving focus broadens exposure to failures and reduces the risk of repeatedly tailoring revisions to the same cases. The evaluation of h0h_{0} on the full 𝒟\mathcal{D} initializes the statistics of every unit. After the formal evaluation of hbh_{b}, the sampler updates the loss of each evaluated unit vv by an exponential moving average:

ℓ¯v(b)=α⁡(1−yv(b))+(1−α)​ℓ¯v(b−1),\bar{\ell}_{v}^{(b)}=\alpha\bigl(1-y_{v}^{(b)}\bigr)+(1-\alpha)\,\bar{\ell}_{v}^{(b-1)}, (4)

where yv(b)∈[0,1]y_{v}^{(b)}\in[0,1] is the score of vv under hbh_{b} and α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1] weights new observations. For a case, yv(b)y_{v}^{(b)} is the mean score of its evaluated queries. A larger α\alpha reacts faster to new failures but is more sensitive to evaluation noise. The sampler also increments the count nvn_{v} of valid observations of vv and records bb as the most recent iteration in which vv was evaluated. For each unit vv in an eligible set 𝒱\mathcal{V}, the sampler then computes a priority rvr_{v} and a sampling probability pvp_{v}:

rv=ℓ¯v+λs​log⁡(1+Δv)+λnnv+1+λu​uv,pv=(1−ϵ)​exp⁡(rv)∑v′∈𝒱exp⁡(rv′)+ϵ|𝒱|.r_{v}=\bar{\ell}_{v}+\lambda_{s}\log(1+\Delta_{v})+\frac{\lambda_{n}}{\sqrt{n_{v}+1}}+\lambda_{u}u_{v},\quad p_{v}=(1-\epsilon)\,\frac{\exp(r_{v})}{\sum_{v^{\prime}\in\mathcal{V}}\exp(r_{v^{\prime}})}+\frac{\epsilon}{|\mathcal{V}|}. (5)

Here, Δv\Delta_{v} is the number of iterations since vv was last evaluated, and uvu_{v} measures how much of its past error has not yet been rechecked. The weights λs\lambda_{s}, λn\lambda_{n}, and λu\lambda_{u} control the contributions of staleness, observation uncertainty, and unresolved errors, respectively. The constant ϵ∈[0,1]\epsilon\in[0,1] reserves probability mass for uniform exploration. The loss and unresolved-error terms focus sampling on failures, whereas the staleness and uncertainty terms and the uniform component preserve coverage. A larger ϵ\epsilon broadens coverage but weakens the focus on failures. The sampler selects units at two levels. It first sets 𝒱=𝒟\mathcal{V}=\mathcal{D} and draws cases according to pvp_{v}. When the selected cases contain more queries than the query cap, it sets 𝒱\mathcal{V} to these queries and applies the same rule to prioritize difficult questions while preserving coverage of the remaining queries.

Adaptive evaluations prioritize actionable failures over estimating overall performance. After budget exhaustion, the Optimizer Agent selects an evaluated candidate from accumulated evidence, prioritizing answer quality over token efficiency. Because sampled subsets differ across iterations and their aggregate scores are not directly comparable, it considers performance on shared cases and queries, coverage, and difficulty. To support this judgment, the Experiment Manager provides comparison tables across evaluations, including performance on common cases and queries, to inform the final selection.

Memory reuse. Memory construction dominates the cost of evaluating a case. However, many edits leave construction unchanged, such as edits confined to retrieval. For a candidate h=hb+1h=h_{b+1}, HoMe identifies the nearest evaluated ancestor h′h^{\prime} with an equivalent construction process by checking that the diff changes no code, prompt, or configuration used during construction. If such an ancestor exists, HoMe reuses its evaluated cases and constructed memory states with probability ρ\rho, rather than always, to account for stochasticity in memory construction. The evaluator restores those memory states and reruns retrieval, answering, and scoring for the new candidate. Otherwise, it resamples and constructs from scratch, enabling broader case coverage and fresh construction outcomes across successive rounds of candidate evaluation.

3.4 Implementation

We implement HoMe on ReMe (Cao et al., 2026), an open-source file-native memory system whose original harness already performs strongly (see Table 1). Improving on this harness therefore provides a stringent test of HoMe. During construction, ReMe extracts information from each session, revises existing content, and writes memory files. In the query stage, it combines retrieval and answering into a single agentic process, in which an Answer Agent repeatedly invokes hybrid search and file-reading tools over the memory files before generating an evidence-grounded answer to the query. Inspired by the Everything-is-a-Plugin design (DeepSeek-AI, 2026), we restructure ReMe into a shared runtime and application-specific plugins. The runtime provides infrastructure unrelated to memory management, such as task execution, model access, and storage. Each plugin instantiates an application-specific harness h=(c,p,θ)h=(c,p,\theta) of the memory system. This separation has two advantages. First, it enables an accurate evaluation of HoMe. The Evaluation Environment runs the same runtime with the candidate plugin, and performance differences on an application thus reflect changes to the harness rather than to the infrastructure. Second, it simplifies evaluation on new applications. Because the runtime instantiates and dispatches registered plugins according to a job configuration, supporting a new application requires only a new plugin. Various memory designs can be easily implemented by replacing the modules, and HoMe can optimize the resulting harnesses through the same evaluation-driven optimization loop, without modifying the framework or its developer-agent workflow.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Benchmarks. We use LongMemEval-S11 1 We use the cleaned LongMemEval-S ground truth released at https://huggingface.co/datasets/agentscope-ai/ReMe_longmemeval_clean_s_v2. (LME) (Wu et al., 2024) and BEAM (Tavakoli et al., 2025). LongMemEval-S contains 500 single-query cases with average 115K history tokens, spanning six question types. All BEAM variants share ten question types, with independent data across variants. BEAM-100K and BEAM-1M contain 20 and 35 cases, respectively, with 20 queries per case and average histories of 131K and 1.04M tokens. The longest BEAM-1M history reaches 1.52M tokens. We randomly split LongMemEval-S equally into training and test sets; for BEAM, we train on BEAM-100K and test on BEAM-1M. All methods are evaluated on the test sets.

Baselines and evaluation. We compare against A-MEM (Xu et al., 2025), SimpleMem (Liu et al., 2026a), ReMe (Cao et al., 2026), and MemPro (Liu et al., 2026c), an automated harness-optimization baseline. We manually tune ReMe separately for each benchmark. For optimization on a given benchmark, both MemPro and HoMe start from the same ReMe harness manually tuned for that benchmark, including in the cross-benchmark transfer experiments. Both methods keep the ReMe runtime fixed and optimize only plugins on the training sets, with their code agents using the same LLM and AgentScope CLI. An LLM judge (Zheng et al., 2023) scores answers following the official protocol. We report all query-stage input and output tokens without deducting KV-cache hits. ReMe-based methods use agentic query loops with growing contexts, allowing more prefix reuse than other methods.

Hyperparameters. We tune the key hyperparameters of SimpleMem and A-MEM on each benchmark’s test set. For SimpleMem, we use (Ksemantic,Kkeyword,Kstructured)=(40,10,10)(K_{\mathrm{semantic}},K_{\mathrm{keyword}},K_{\mathrm{structured}})=(40,10,10) on LongMemEval-S and (35,8,8)(35,8,8) on BEAM, with at most three reflection rounds. For A-MEM, the retrieval count KK is 1616 on LongMemEval-S and 1010 on BEAM. MemPro performs up to eight formal evaluations, using the same 50 training cases sampled once at the start on LongMemEval-S and the full training set in every round on BEAM. For HoMe, we set the formal evaluation budget to B=6B=6 and concurrency to 28. Each evaluation uses 28 cases on LongMemEval-S or 100 queries from 10 cases on BEAM. We set α=0.3\alpha=0.3 in Eq. 4, ϵ=0.2\epsilon=0.2 in Eq. 5, and memory reuse probability ρ=0.6\rho=0.6. Across all methods, memory construction uses qwen3.6-flash, all other LLM calls use qwen3.7-max, and embeddings use Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B.

4.2 Main Results

4.2.1 Optimization Effectiveness

HoMe achieves the highest answer score on both benchmarks (Table 1). Relative to the initial ReMe harness, the LongMemEval-S score rises from 0.888 to 0.916 as query-stage tokens fall from 43.9K to 17.9K. On BEAM-1M, the score rises from 0.650 to 0.704 as tokens fall from 101.8K to 60.4K, even though test histories are about 8×8\times longer on average than those used for optimization. Token savings accompany fewer LLM calls on LongMemEval-S (4.7 to 3.0 per query) and fewer tokens per call on BEAM, where calls increase from 4.5 to 6.7. A second independent BEAM search reaches 0.720 at 68.3K tokens per query under the same settings, again improving both metrics over ReMe (Appendix A.4). Relative to ReMe, gains are largest on LongMemEval-S single-session preference and BEAM contradiction resolution, while scores decline on LongMemEval-S multi-session questions and BEAM knowledge update and information extraction; per-category results and statistical comparisons are provided in Appendix A.1. Compared with MemPro, HoMe raises answer scores by 10.4 pp on LongMemEval-S and 1.1 pp on BEAM, while reducing query-stage tokens by 81.5% and 7.6%, respectively.

We transfer the selected harness to the target benchmark without further optimization. HoMe transfers in both directions with higher scores and fewer tokens than MemPro (Table 2). The harness optimized on BEAM-100K reaches 0.908 on LongMemEval-S at 26.6K tokens per query, improving on both MemPro (0.800 at 42.2K) and the initial ReMe harness (0.888 at 43.9K). The harness optimized on LongMemEval-S reaches 0.639 on BEAM-1M at 39.0K tokens per query, compared with 0.617 at 113.1K for MemPro. Relative to ReMe, it uses 62% fewer tokens at a 1.1 pp lower score and remains on the Pareto frontier.

MemPro’s candidates modify only prompts or parameters, and its training-selected harness scores 0.812 on the LongMemEval-S test set compared with 0.888 for its starting harness (Appendix A.6). HoMe uses shared failure mechanisms identified across cases to guide code changes to source allocation, evidence selection, and cross-session indexing (Section 4.3). Across all candidates, its LongMemEval-S and BEAM runs make 1,379 and 1,242 line edits, respectively, spanning code, prompts, and configuration (Tables 6 and 7).

4.2.2 Optimization Efficiency

On BEAM, HoMe completes optimization in 10.4 hours, compared with 11 hours 23 minutes for MemPro. Under high API concurrency, wall-clock times are sensitive to network fluctuations and rate limiting. Total optimization token consumption is 185.2M for HoMe versus 331.2M for MemPro, a 44.1% reduction. We examine this efficiency in terms of optimization iterations, evaluation workload, and time per evaluation.

Strong harnesses emerge within a few iterations. Figure 3 shows the evaluation results of BEAM candidates on the full training set, measured retrospectively after optimization. The second candidate lies on the Pareto frontier, and candidates two through four offer different trade-offs, reaching a score up to 0.73 or a query cost as low as 31.8K tokens. The optimization discovers competitive harnesses within only a few iterations. The final two candidates do not extend the frontier, indicating that additional iterations may not make improvements. As edits accumulate, optimization may become more sensitive to random variation in sampled evaluations and more prone to overfitting.

Adaptive sampling reduces evaluation workload. On BEAM, each formal evaluation uses 10 cases and 100 queries, representing 50% fewer cases and 75% fewer queries than MemPro. On LongMemEval-S, HoMe evaluates 28 cases per iteration compared with MemPro’s 50, a 44% reduction. With smaller evaluations, HoMe achieves higher test scores and fewer query-time tokens than MemPro on both benchmarks (Table 1). Because the sampled subsets differ across candidates and prioritize historically difficult units, their aggregate answer scores are not directly comparable. HoMe therefore relies on the Optimizer Agent to judge candidate answer quality from accumulated evaluation evidence, considering shared-case/query comparisons, coverage, and difficulty. Across six BEAM candidates, sampled and full-set query-token reductions are positively correlated (Pearson r=0.870r=0.870), suggesting that sampled evaluations reflect full-set token savings.

Formal evaluation time falls sharply. Table 3 shows cumulative time savings per formal evaluation. Parallelism reduces full evaluation time by over 90%; sampling reduces case counts, and reuse avoids reconstruction. Reuse saves 94% on LongMemEval-S, reflecting the construction cost of single-query cases, and applies to five LongMemEval-S candidates and four BEAM candidates. These per-evaluation savings do not include the initial full evaluation, diagnosis, editing, and debugging that also contribute to total optimization time. HoMe reaches the BEAM Pareto frontier after 6.3 hours.

4.3 Case Study

HoMe modifies memory structures, code, and the system prompt. Figure 3 illustrates four revisions that change the evidence available to the Answer Agent. The first two were independently discovered on different datasets, while the last two are specific to LongMemEval-S and BEAM, respectively. Additional improvements and the failure patterns they address in each benchmark are described in Appendix A.2.

  1. Case 1:

    Improving cross-session evidence coverage. The Diagnoser Agent found recurring errors on summarization and enumeration questions spanning multiple dates. Hybrid search retrieved relevant passages but missed pertinent sessions within its small retrieval window. Daily topic summaries competed with raw conversations and were not reliably retrieved. The Optimizer Agent modified the search tool to compile summaries into a compact, date-grouped topic list. The answering prompt directs the Answer Agent to survey this list for relevant sessions across dates, avoiding repeated searches that cover only part of the question.

  2. Case 2:

    Diversifying the retrieval window. The Diagnoser Agent observed that hybrid search often retrieved multiple chunks from the same file. Long raw transcripts occupied several slots, reducing source diversity. The Optimizer Agent introduced per-file slot limits, stricter for raw transcripts than for memory notes. Once a file reaches its limit, chunks from other files fill the remaining slots. This gives the Answer Agent evidence from more sources within the same retrieval budget.

  3. Case 3:

    Indexing user actions on LongMemEval-S. The Diagnoser Agent found that many questions require precise user-action details buried in broader session notes. The Optimizer Agent added a line summarizing the user’s own actions to each note during construction. A separate inverted index over these lines lets the Answer Agent search action descriptions for notes containing potentially relevant evidence.

  4. Case 4:

    Compressing retrieved evidence on BEAM. To reduce retrieved context, the Optimizer Agent introduced query-guided line selection within retrieved chunks. The search tool scores lines by question keywords and replaces lower-scoring lines with placeholders preserving line numbers. The Answer Agent receives shorter results and can use the line numbers to recover omitted text when a passage requires closer inspection. Retaining source paths and line numbers thus reduces query-time tokens while keeping omitted evidence accessible through targeted reads on demand.

These studies show how cross-case diagnosis leads to new retrieval mechanisms and memory structures. Independent optimization runs on both benchmarks found related mechanisms, suggesting that source diversity and broader access to stored evidence may offer general design principles for memory systems. The benchmark-specific changes show that HoMe can identify distinctive patterns in each dataset’s questions and histories and adapt the harness. By changing which evidence the Answer Agent sees and how much text it must inspect, these mechanisms improve evidence utilization and enable token savings, supporting the stronger trade-offs between scores and token consumption observed in the main and transfer results.

5 Conclusion

This paper presents HoMe, an evaluation-driven framework that guides free-form harness revisions through cross-case diagnosis and early structural exploration. HoMe traces failures to the responsible sessions and harness components through session-level memory versioning and reduces evaluation cost of candidate harnesses through smoke tests, candidate gating, adaptive sampling, and memory reuse. With only six evaluated candidates per benchmark, HoMe extends the strong original harness of ReMe with new mechanisms such as fact-level memory indexes and source-aware retrieval. The resulting harnesses improve end-task accuracy by 2.8 pp while reducing query-time tokens by 59% on LongMemEval-S, and by 5.4 pp while reducing query-time tokens by 41% on BEAM-1M. These results show that HoMe makes automated harness optimization practical even for strong memory systems.

A.1 Detailed Results

We randomly split LongMemEval-S into equally sized training and test sets. The 250 training case IDs are listed in the ReMe split configuration. The remaining 250 cases form the test set.

Statistical comparisons with ReMe. On BEAM-1M, the score improves by 0.054 (paired bootstrap 95% CI: [0.028,0.082][0.028,0.082], p=0.0002p=0.0002), a statistically significant gain. Query-token consumption also decreases significantly, by approximately 41.4K tokens per query (40.7%; query-level paired bootstrap 95% CI for the difference: [−47,073,−35,389][-47{,}073,-35{,}389], p<10−4p<10^{-4}). On LongMemEval-S, the score shows a modest improvement of 0.028, although this gain does not reach statistical significance (paired bootstrap 95% CI: [−0.016,0.072][-0.016,0.072], p=0.25p=0.25). Alongside this modest score gain, query-token consumption decreases significantly, by 26,057 tokens per query (59.3%; two-sample bootstrap 95% CI for the difference: [−32,741,−19,674][-32{,}741,-19{,}674], p<10−4p<10^{-4}).

Per-category results. A.2 Case Studies of HoMe

This appendix summarizes memory harness improvements from the LongMemEval-S and BEAM optimization runs, focusing on the failures they address and the mechanisms behind them.

A.2.1 LongMemEval-S: Fact Recall, Aggregate Retrieval, and Answer Calibration

  1. 1.

    Write short, self-contained user facts instead of topic-oriented essays. Baseline notes often devoted space to generic advice while losing exact dates, numbers, or the option the user actually chose. The surrounding generic text also diluted the embedding representation of specific facts. The revised construction policy prioritized complete user states, preferences, decisions, and feelings; preserved session-specific names, dates, and prices verbatim; and compressed generic explanations to a line. It aimed for one note per session, beginning with self-contained key user facts. This reduced overlapping notes and made important facts more likely to survive chunking and be retrieved on their own. When a length budget is tight, generic background should be removed before user facts.

  2. 2.

    Control both semantic duplication and concentration by source in a small window. Similar notes from one session can consume nearly every retrieval slot. Multiple chunks from one transcript can also occupy several slots before rendering merges them into a single displayed item, leaving no room for a different source. The first problem was addressed with relevance-heavy maximal marginal relevance: highly similar candidates receive a modest penalty while strong retrieval scores still dominate. The second was addressed by capping the slots taken by each file, with a stricter cap for raw transcripts than for notes. Both mechanisms postpone excess candidates rather than deleting them. The useful accounting unit is the distinct evidence ultimately delivered, not merely the number of retrieved chunks.

  3. 3.

    Add an inexpensive catalog index beyond top-k retrieval. A question such as “How many times did I attend a graduation?” requires every occurrence, whereas a similarity search guarantees only the most similar few. Each note already has a title and a one-line description, so the system can scan this compact catalog across all notes, match query terms, and append a candidate list to normal search results. A document-frequency threshold removes generic template words such as “user”; ranking uses the strongest discriminative term rather than allowing many weak matches to accumulate. Each entry keeps its path and a description excerpt around the match, telling the agent which note to inspect. The index addresses a coverage gap in top-k retrieval while leaving semantic search in place.

  4. 4.

    Extend the catalog to individual facts while retaining both levels. A one-line description is necessarily lossy: an additional graduation, a particular island, or a precise bedtime may appear only in the note body. The expanded index scans notes and splits self-contained Markdown list items into fact entries. Matching entries are quoted inline, allowing the agent to use the fact without another read call. Fact and catalog layers calculate term frequencies and rankings separately, so adding the finer layer does not silently change how the coarser one behaves. Facts already visible in the normal retrieval window are suppressed in the index to avoid duplication. The catalog remains useful because a question phrased in terms of a session’s topic may share no content word with the answer sentence. The layers answer complementary questions: “Which note might matter?” and “Which statement in it matters?”

  5. 5.

    Keep the inexpensive index available, vary its width, and state what a match proves. The run briefly gated index delivery to enumeration questions or explicit requests to reduce irrelevant matches. Case-by-case inspection showed that the gate did not cause the improvements initially attributed to it; withholding the index instead prompted repeated blind query rewrites and higher total token use. The final design kept the index available for every question, returned a shorter list for point queries and a wider one for enumeration, and warned in the index header that keyword overlap is only a lead. A nonempty list does not establish that the entity or event in the question exists; each entry must be checked against the requested fact. Query wording alone did not predict where evidence was stored. For a cheap index, controlling output size and clarifying evidential meaning proved more useful than gating access by question form.

  6. 6.

    Diagnose “the evidence was found” separately from “the answer was correct.” In several cases the agent read the right note but abstained because it demanded a completion confirmation that memory would never record. In others, it corrected a false premise yet still supplied the value that the false premise requested. Answering rules were calibrated to anchor relative times, use newer records for current state, respect entity boundaries, and reject the requested value when its premise is false. Rules without case-level evidence were later removed because their prompt cost recurred at every ReAct step. A memory answer can fail at construction, retrieval, evidence interpretation, or final decision. More retrieved material is unlikely to repair a decision error once the correct evidence is already visible.

A.2.2 BEAM: Coverage, Order, and Access to Evidence in Long Conversations

  1. 1.

    Reserve room for both curated memory and primary evidence in the retrieval window. The system stores condensed notes alongside verbatim transcripts, which account for roughly 95% of indexed chunks. A window filled solely by the highest-scoring chunks is therefore easily dominated by transcripts, leaving out the notes that integrate information across passages. The optimized ranking favors notes while reserving slots for transcripts, so the answering agent can use the consolidated account and still check exact wording, numbers, and chronology. This rearrangement changes the order of candidates without discarding any. Crucially, it happens before the system marks returned chunks as seen: otherwise, a chunk displaced from the window could be recorded as already shown and become unreachable in later searches. In a mixed memory store, the source composition of the window matters as much as the ranking of individual chunks.

  2. 2.

    Compress search responses without cutting off access to the original text. Long transcript chunks make repeated searches expensive, yet a simple truncation can hide the line containing the answer. The first measure placed a character budget on responses while retaining the path and line range for each result; text that did not fit remained available through an explicit pointer for targeted reading. When truncation from the beginning repeatedly omitted facts in the middle or end of a note, selection moved to the line level. Lines were scored using the distinctiveness of query terms, numbers, and heading cues. The budget first covered multiple evidence-bearing lines, then used any remaining space for adjacent context. When a semantic match had no lexical overlap, the title and summary were still retained. Effective compression thus has two requirements: show the most useful evidence now, and make every omitted passage straightforward to locate later.

  3. 3.

    Give coverage questions a global view instead of repeatedly enlarging top-k. Answers to questions such as “Which topics did I mention?” may be spread across many sessions. Similarity search can return highly relevant chunks without establishing that all matching occurrences have been found. The optimizer therefore derived a compact chronological index from all notes, appended it to ordinary retrieval results, and delivered it automatically at most once per question. Entries carried paths for verification. Near-duplicate entries from overlapping notes in one session were consolidated while their paths remained accessible. To control cost, automatic delivery was routed only for coverage questions after offline checks. A measured regression exposed the index’s limit: a thematic summary can look sufficient for a question about the first-mention order while omitting precisely the ordering evidence needed to answer it. A global index can support “what was mentioned” without automatically serving as an answer to “in what order.”

  4. 4.

    For ordering questions, provide a reading route rather than a summary that invites an immediate answer. Ordering evidence spans dates and sessions, so one note seldom contains all relevant mentions. An earlier summary-style index encouraged the agent to answer from its overview, saving tokens but getting the sequence wrong. The revised route listed note paths in chronological order and then annotated each path with the line range of its conversation-flow section. The agent could read the passages that recorded mention order and speaker identity without loading every entire note. Those sections occupied about 30% of a note on average, making broader coverage feasible within the tool and context budgets. An index need only guide reading; when the answer depends on fine-grained order, compressing evidence into a topical summary can remove the deciding information.

  5. 5.

    Record relationships at construction time that retrieval cannot reconstruct. Case-level traces showed failures in which the relevant note had been found, but the note never preserved who made a statement, when a topic first appeared, or whether a new statement superseded an older one. Construction rules were revised to identify the speaker, distinguish an assistant’s suggestion from a user’s decision, retain a conversation-flow record in actual mention order, preserve enduring instructions verbatim, and keep both sides of an update with an explicit supersession relation. Retrieval can reorder stored text; it cannot recover attribution, order, or update relations discarded during compression. The questions a memory system must answer should therefore inform the structure of what it writes.

Together, these runs show that memory optimization reaches beyond vector ranking. Construction determines which relationships remain recoverable; the retrieval window determines which sources fit within a budget; derived indexes address the coverage limits of top-k search; and answer policy determines how evidence is used. When evaluation rounds sample different cases, contributions of individual mechanisms are best assessed through paired questions and execution traces, particularly when several changes were introduced together.

A.3 Optimization Trajectories of HoMe 

Tables 6 and 7 summarize the candidates proposed in each optimization run. Scores are measured on sampled training questions; ⋆\star marks the final harness selected by the Optimizer Agent. Elapsed is the cumulative wall-clock time at the completion of each iteration, including diagnosis, candidate generation, evaluation, and the initial evaluation reused by these runs. The initial evaluation took 5 hours 30 minutes on LongMemEval-S and 87 minutes on BEAM. Line counts compare each candidate with its predecessor. In the Changed column, cc, pp, and θ\theta denote changes to code, prompts, and configuration, respectively. The reported times mark the completion of each evaluation; the total optimization time also includes the agent’s final harness selection after the last evaluation.

A.4 Stability

Two independent BEAM searches with the same initial harness, hyperparameters, and evaluation budget produce stable gains: the final harnesses score 0.704 and 0.720 on BEAM-1M, using 60.4K and 68.3K query-stage tokens, respectively. Both improve on ReMe and lie on the empirical Pareto frontier (Figure 4). Paired bootstrap resampling over the same BEAM-1M test queries shows significant gains over ReMe (0.650) for both runs. The improvements are +0.054 (95% CI: [0.028, 0.082], p=0.0002p=0.0002) and +0.070 (95% CI: [0.042, 0.090], p<0.0001p<0.0001), respectively.

Consistency extends to both diagnoses and proposed improvements (Table 8). Both runs identify similar construction and retrieval defects and propose related changes to evidence selection, indexing, and information preservation, although their implementations differ.

This stability is supported by independent case investigations and cross-case synthesis, which reduce the influence of individual attribution errors. Git preserves promising alternatives, while gating encourages mechanism exploration before refinement, reducing premature convergence on local prompt patches.

A.5 Detailed Execution Trace of Harness Optimization

This appendix traces a supplementary BEAM-100K optimization run through evaluation, delegated investigation, cross-case diagnosis, implementation, and evaluation. The Optimizer first requests a diagnosis of the initial evaluation. The Diagnoser examines evaluation artifacts and delegates selected failures to Case Study Agents, then synthesizes their findings into shared harness defects. The Optimizer implements a candidate; evaluation exposes an overly aggressive intervention, which it subsequently narrows and re-evaluates. All reported versions use the same 200 training queries from 10 cases. Quotations reproduce persisted instructions, analyses, and reports, with omissions marked by […][\ldots].

Evaluation and delegation: the Optimizer requests mechanism-level diagnosis.

The initial harness scored 0.6120. After inspecting its code and evaluation artifacts, the Optimizer invoked home_diagnose, asking the Diagnoser to distinguish construction, retrieval, and answering failures:

“Identify the distinct root causes of low-scoring queries. Specifically: (1) Is memory construction (auto_memory daily notes) losing information needed by the queries, or is retrieval/routing at query time failing to surface existing memory? […][\ldots] what evidence patterns distinguish failure modes such as ‘correct memory exists but not retrieved’, ‘retrieved but wrong answer’, ‘memory never written’, ‘answered Information not found when answer existed’? Rank directions by impact and coverage.”

The Diagnoser operated in a separate, read-only investigation context. Its instructions explicitly required “Do NOT prescribe or implement fixes,” leaving implementation decisions to the Optimizer.

Investigation: the Diagnoser delegates concrete failures to Case Study Agents.

The Diagnoser first aggregated all 200 query records, including scores, answers, search/read calls, retrieved file paths, and judge feedback. It then submitted six selected cases (1, 5, 9, 12, 14, and 19) to home_case_study, executed with four-way concurrency. The shared investigation instruction required evidence-level tracing for low-scoring queries:

“For each query in this case scoring below 0.5, determine the lifecycle stage where the point was lost, using concrete evidence with absolute file paths, query ids and short quotes. […][\ldots] does the information the golden answer requires exist in the exported memory workspace […][\ldots]? […][\ldots] did the agent’s search/read tool calls actually surface that information […][\ldots]? Report per query id, then summarize the dominant mechanism(s) for this case and any evidence that contradicts them. Do not propose fixes.”

For example, the Case 5 investigator used home_inspect_evaluation and home_trace_query_evidence, inspected answer logs and daily notes, and compared them with the original sessions. The following excerpts show two different attribution outcomes.

Case Study Agent evidence: related content is mistaken for support, while other evidence is never retrieved.

For Case 5, abstention:2, the question asked about specific feedback received after quizzes. The investigator compared the requested detail with the memory content:

“Memory state: Memory notes mention ‘88% quiz accuracy on 12 dependent-event problems’ (daily/2024-02-15/probability-concepts-and-learning-progress.md) but no specific feedback received after quizzes. The quiz scores exist but not post-quiz feedback. […][\ldots] Root cause: Answer generation failure; agent could not distinguish ‘quiz score data exists’ from ‘feedback after quizzes exists.’ Never attempted to verify absence.”

This finding localized the error beyond a generic retrieval failure: the answer substituted an adjacent fact for the specific information requested.

The Case 12 investigator found a different failure in contradiction_resolution:1, which asked whether the user had read books by Daniel Dennett:

“Memory exists: Session 1 contains both statements: Line 64: ‘I started reading “Elbow Room” by Daniel Dennett on March 13’ (retrieved) Line 69: ‘I’ve never read any books by Daniel Dennett’ (NOT retrieved) […][\ldots] Root cause: Retrieval failure; the ‘never read’ statement at session/dialog/beam_100K_12_batch1.jsonl:69 was never retrieved despite existing in memory.”

The two reports therefore distinguished unsupported answering from missing retrieval coverage, using the requested detail, stored evidence, and actual search results rather than the final score alone.

Diagnoser synthesis: connect local findings to shared harness defects.

The Diagnoser combined the case reports with aggregate evidence and inspected the pinned harness code. For abstention failures, it identified a recurring chain:

“query targets a detail that was never stated →\rightarrow search legitimately returns adjacent topic content →\rightarrow […][\ldots] retrieved adjacency is treated as ‘found’ →\rightarrow agent quotes/extends adjacent text →\rightarrow rubric requires refusal →\rightarrow 0.”

Inspection of agentic_answer.yaml linked this behavior to the answering policy:

“There is no rule to reject an unsupported premise or to abstain when adjacent-but-non-answering content is retrieved, and no rule about contradicting an implied premise.”

For contradiction handling, the Diagnoser separated failures to retrieve both statements from failures to use evidence already retrieved. Its report identified the latter pattern across cases:

“prompt mentions conflicting information only as a search instruction […][\ldots] and never as an answer rule →\rightarrow both statements are retrieved but the agent resolves to a single value […][\ldots].

Both-sides-retrieved-and-still-wrong: case19 contradiction_resolution:2 retrieved session/dialog/beam_100K_19_batch2.jsonl:13 and beam_100K_19_batch3.jsonl:73-74 in the same context and answered ‘Yes.’ […][\ldots] Retrieval-side subset: case12 contradiction_resolution:1 (0.25) retrieved line 64 but never line 69 of beam_100K_12_batch1.jsonl.”

This synthesis gave the Optimizer a more precise target: evidence sufficiency and conflict handling required explicit answering mechanisms, while some failures still required retrieval improvements.

Implementation and evaluation feedback: the Optimizer introduces an audit mechanism.

Using the diagnosis, the Optimizer implemented d003d84, adding a post-retrieval evidence auditor alongside answering-policy and timeline-grounding changes. The auditor reconstructed source passages from the search ledger, made one bounded LLM call, and returned structured fields including detail_status, conflicts, later_statement_supersedes, and confidence. Its gate could replace the draft with an abstention or a response presenting conflicting statements. The complete patch changed four files, with +609/−3+609/-3 lines.

The candidate-admission reviewer accepted the executable mechanism:

“Adds real runtime mechanisms, not prompt tuning: […][\ldots] _evidence_audit re-materializes the chunks the agent actually retrieved from the tool-context dedup ledger […][\ldots] runs one extra bounded LLM verification call […][\ldots] and gate_answer can override response.answer with an abstention or surfaced contradiction.”

Construction-equivalence review confirmed that the changes were confined to the query path. After passing the smoke test, the candidate was evaluated using the initial constructed memory. Its score fell to 0.4762, exposing a defect in the new intervention.

Feedback-driven repair: restrict the auditor’s authority.

The Optimizer paired the recorded audit decisions with query outcomes and identified the harmful branch:

“The d003d84 gate’s ABSTENTION override was catastrophic: fired 72×\times, base 0.586 →\rightarrow cand 0.101. It cannot distinguish ‘detail not recorded’ from ‘answer requires synthesis across adjacent records’: event_ordering 18/20 overridden, multi_session_reasoning 14/20 […][\ldots].”

The auditor read at most 3,000 characters per file and 12,000 characters overall; the report recorded that “54 of 72 earlier verdicts were clipped at the cap.” A limited-view sufficiency judgment was therefore being given authority to suppress an answer requiring synthesis. For contradiction overrides, the Optimizer found another useful distinction:

“CONTRADICTION override split cleanly by whether the DRAFT already acknowledged a conflict: ack & conflicts = 5/5 wins […][\ldots]; conflicts where draft was silent = losses […][\ldots].”

The resulting commit, b08d48a, removed the entire abstention-override path and added draft_acknowledges_conflict(). Contradiction formatting now required confidence ≥0.75\geq 0.75, a genuine conflict not superseded by a later statement, and acknowledgement of disagreement in the draft. The patch changed two files, with +46/−45+46/-45 lines: functional edits to _evidence_audit.py and module-documentation edits to agentic_answer.py. The existing answering prompt was retained.

Re-evaluation: measure the repaired harness.

Construction-equivalence review again returned construction_unchanged. The host nevertheless selected reconstruction under its probabilistic evaluation policy. The repaired candidate passed the smoke test and was formally evaluated with newly constructed memory.

Relative to the initial harness, the repaired version improved the score by 6.4 points and reduced mean query tokens by 11.7%. Paired results comprised 51 improvements, 28 regressions, and 121 ties; eight of ten cases improved. Abstention scores rose from 0.400 to 0.650 and contradiction-resolution scores from 0.456 to 0.625, while knowledge-update scores declined from 0.750 to 0.625. The trace records both the delegated diagnosis that motivated the executable mechanism and the evaluation feedback that led the Optimizer to correct its implementation.

A.6 Optimization Trajectories of MemPro

We inspect MemPro candidates from our ReMe-based BEAM-100K and LongMemEval-S runs. BM0 and LM0 denote the initial harnesses. Changed denotes prompts pp, parameters θ\theta, or code-level mechanism changes cc. All scores are training scores.

A.6.1 BEAM-100K

All eight candidates modify prompts only: seven edit the answering prompt (agentic_answer.yaml) and one edits the memory-construction prompt (auto_memory.yaml). None modifies executable pipeline logic, tool implementations, or index structures.

  1. 1.

    BM1: Search guidance. Adds three instructions covering exact entity names and aliases, temporal context, and checks for current and previous attribute values.

  2. 2.

    BM2: Temporal memory preservation. Adds one construction-prompt principle requiring chronological markers and dated records of previous and updated attribute values.

  3. 3.

    BM3: Strict abstention. Adds six lines requiring direct evidence, discouraging synthesis from loosely related fragments, and favoring abstention under uncertainty. The score falls from 0.6589 to 0.6050.

  4. 4.

    BM4: Branching and balanced abstention. Branches from BM2, adding two search instructions for contradictory evidence and separate sessions. Replaces one abstention rule with three allowing evidence synthesis while withholding unsupported details.

  5. 5.

    BM5: Detail-sensitive abstention and chronology. Replaces one temporal-search instruction and two abstention rules and adds an event-ordering rule. Distinguishes topical relevance from evidence for specific details and searches each event separately before assembling a chronology in draft notes.

  6. 6.

    BM6: Explicit contradiction handling. Replaces one search instruction to emphasize supporting and opposing evidence; adds an answer rule to describe cross-session contradictions explicitly.

  7. 7.

    BM7: Prompt consolidation. Consolidates search and answer instructions into 14 nonempty lines, shortening the prompt by approximately 1.2K characters. Adds a completeness rule for planning, recommendation, and implementation requests. Exact added/deleted counts are unavailable because the edit record omits deleted lines.

  8. 8.

    BM8: Cross-session and numerical search. Adds two instructions: search sessions or periods separately, and check current and previous numerical values or status updates.

After a failed direction and recovery through branching, BM8 achieves the highest score, 0.6933.

A.6.2 LongMemEval-S

Six candidates edit agentic_answer.yaml; three adjust parameters in plugin.yaml or search_v2.py, with LM4 doing both. None introduces a code-level mechanism change.

  1. 1.

    LM1: Entity, temporal, and cross-session search. Rewrites search guidance to use entity names and aliases, search events or sessions separately, and retrieve current and historical values. Answer rules prioritize recent explicit statements and retain dated old and new values for change questions.

  2. 2.

    LM2: Date filtering and exhaustive counting. Adds three instructions: convert relative time windows to absolute dates, resolve relative weekdays before narrow date-filtered searches, and enumerate all matching instances before counting instead of abstaining prematurely.

  3. 3.

    LM3: Search persistence. Branches from LM0. Requires two or three searches, query reformulation, cross-checking, and broader queries for sparse results.

  4. 4.

    LM4: Temporal guidance, counting, and retrieval limit. Adds relative-to-absolute date guidance and counting rules requiring multiple queries and itemized draft notes. Raises _DEFAULT_LIMIT in search_v2.py from 5 to 10, changing a parameter rather than retrieval logic.

  5. 5.

    LM5: Stronger counting persistence. Requires four or five query variants and five or six searches before abstention, combines item types with action verbs, records dates and sources in drafts, and retries without date filters. The score falls from 0.840 to 0.820.

  6. 6.

    LM6: Larger pre-reranking candidate pool. Branches from LM4, increasing only candidate_multiplier in plugin.yaml from 5.0 to 8.0. The score rises to 0.860.

  7. 7.

    LM7: Query-formulation examples. Branches from LM4, adding combinations of entities and actions, singular/plural variants, date calculations, and failed-case examples: “coffee maker,” “faucet,” and “toaster.” The score falls to 0.780.

  8. 8.

    LM8: Retrieval-default adjustments. Branches from LM6, raising _DEFAULT_LIMIT from 10 to 15 and synchronizing the code’s default candidate_multiplier to 8.0; only defaults change.

The search returns to stronger parents after regressions. LM6 and LM8 tie at 0.860, and LM8 is selected for test evaluation.

A.6.3 Analysis

Across these two ReMe-based runs, all sixteen MemPro candidates modify prompts or parameters without introducing new code-level mechanisms. BEAM revisions focus on search and abstention guidance; LongMemEval-S revisions also adjust retrieval limits and candidate-pool size. Both trajectories show gains and regressions across iterations. These observations motivate explicit cross-case diagnosis and candidate gating to guide structural exploration under a limited budget.

A.7 Adaptive Sampling Details

The initial full training-set evaluation initializes a sampling record for each case and query. For a sampling unit vv, the record contains its exponential moving average of loss ℓ¯v\bar{\ell}_{v}, number of valid score observations nvn_{v}, most recent selected round tvselt_{v}^{\mathrm{sel}}, most recent error round tverrt_{v}^{\mathrm{err}}, and number kvk_{v} of perfect-score observations since that error. Only valid scores update ℓ¯v\bar{\ell}_{v} and nvn_{v}. A case-level observation is the mean score of the queries evaluated for that case in the current round.

After observing score yv(b)y_{v}^{(b)} in round bb, the sampler updates

ℓ¯v←{1−yv(b),nv=0,α⁡(1−yv(b))+(1−α)​ℓ¯v,nv>0,nv←nv+1.\bar{\ell}_{v}\leftarrow\begin{cases}1-y_{v}^{(b)},&n_{v}=0,\\ \alpha(1-y_{v}^{(b)})+(1-\alpha)\bar{\ell}_{v},&n_{v}>0,\end{cases}\qquad n_{v}\leftarrow n_{v}+1. (6)

A score below 11 sets tverr=bt_{v}^{\mathrm{err}}=b and kv=0k_{v}=0; a perfect score after an earlier error increments kvk_{v}. Units without a valid observation retain their loss estimate and observation count.

For a unit eligible in round bb, let Δv=max⁡(b−tvsel,0)\Delta_{v}=\max(b-t_{v}^{\mathrm{sel}},0). The unresolved-error term in the sampling priority is

uv={0,if v has no recorded error,log⁡(1+max⁡(b−tverr,0))1+kv,otherwise.u_{v}=\begin{cases}0,&\text{if $v$ has no recorded error},\\[5.69054pt] \dfrac{\log\!\left(1+\max(b-t_{v}^{\mathrm{err}},0)\right)}{1+k_{v}},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (7)

The priority weights are fixed at λs=0.2\lambda_{s}=0.2, λn=0.2\lambda_{n}=0.2, and λu=0.1\lambda_{u}=0.1. For the eligible set 𝒱\mathcal{V}, the sampling probability is

pv=(1−ϵ)​exp⁡(rv)∑v′∈𝒱exp⁡(rv′)+ϵ|𝒱|,p_{v}=(1-\epsilon)\frac{\exp(r_{v})}{\sum_{v^{\prime}\in\mathcal{V}}\exp(r_{v^{\prime}})}+\frac{\epsilon}{|\mathcal{V}|}, (8)

where rvr_{v} is the priority defined in the main text.

The moving-average loss favors currently difficult units, while the staleness term revisits units that have not been tested against recent harness changes. The observation-count term gives less frequently measured units additional opportunity to be sampled. The unresolved-error term retains attention on an earlier failure until subsequent perfect-score observations reduce its contribution. Logarithmic staleness growth prevents age alone from increasing priority linearly, and the uniform component gives every eligible unit a nonzero chance of exposing a new regression. These terms are sampling heuristics rather than estimates of statistical uncertainty.

Sampling proceeds at two levels. The sampler first sets 𝒱=𝒟\mathcal{V}=\mathcal{D} and draws cases without replacement according to pvp_{v}. If the queries in the selected cases exceed the per-iteration query cap, it sets 𝒱\mathcal{V} to the queries in those cases and applies the same sampling rule at the query level. Otherwise, it evaluates all their queries. Both levels deliberately favor historically difficult units. Consequently, the resulting score is useful for finding failures and guiding revisions, but should not be interpreted as an unbiased estimate of a candidate’s full-training-set performance.

A.8 Search Token Consumption on BEAM-100K

We report total optimization token consumption on BEAM-100K by stage and model. For both methods, counts include all LLM input and output tokens from evaluations (including formal evaluations and smoke tests) and developer agents throughout optimization, without discounting cache hits. Embedding tokens and supplementary experiments outside the optimization runs are excluded.

HoMe uses 44.1% fewer search tokens than MemPro. Construction and query tokens decrease by 45.4% and 59.0%, respectively. Although HoMe spends more tokens on developer agents, sampling and construction reuse reduce the dominant evaluation workload.

A.9 System Prompts of HoMe 

HoMe instantiates five LLM agents around the optimization loop: the optimizer agent, which proposes candidate memory mechanisms and drives the cycle of editing, debugging, and validation; the diagnostic agent, a read-only diagnostician that ranks evidence-supported root causes of evaluation failures; the case-study agent, which traces a single failed evaluation case backward through judging, retrieval, construction, and source code; the candidate admission gate, which decides whether a committed change merits an early formal evaluation slot; and the construction-equivalence reviewer, which decides whether a candidate may reuse the persisted memory-construction workspace of its base commit.
